newsitem.title: USA: Dole gets rained out in New Jersey battleground state.
newsitem.headline: Dole gets rained out in New Jersey battleground state.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole's effort on Tuesday to convince voters in the battleground state of New Jersey that he is more trustworthy than President Bill Clinton was mostly drowned out by a tropical storm.

On his bus tour through the state, Dole held two brief and sparsely attended campaign rallies -- one damp, one soaked -- and in hastily arranged stops he shook hands at a diner and coached senior citizens playing cards at a church social hall.

But he had to cancel two more rallies and a fundraiser to fly home to Washington ahead of the remnants of tropical storm Josephine, the second time a major storm had disrupted a Dole trip to this pivotal state with its 15 electoral votes.
The day's most memorable moment came when a boisterous backer reached out to shake Dole's hand after the Lyndhurst rally and shouted, "Please get Bozo out of the White House."

"Bozo's on his way out," replied Dole, who has boasted of trying to stick to the issues and avoid name-calling, but who evidently could not resist the temptation to liken Clinton to the well-known U.S. television clown.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said of the Bozo remark, "It's not hard to imagine that Senator Dole might be feeling a little desperate at this point."

But he noted that Dole had "gained some ground in front of the American people by being humorous, by being respectful and by conducting himself in a civil manner on Sunday night," in the candidates' debate.
At every opportunity he had during the rain-soaked day, Dole depicted himself as more trustworthy than Clinton and his "empty promises."
"This election is about keeping your word. It is about trust. Who do you want in charge of the White House as we go into the next century," Dole told the rally in Morristown.

"I can give you example after example after example (when) Clinton said one thing and did another," Dole told the other rally. "You can ask any of my collegues who served with me in the Congress, Democrat or Republican, and one thing they'll tell you. When Bob Dole gives you his word you can go to the bank with it. It's good. He won't change his mind."

Dole had planned a two-day trip in his "Asphalt One" bus -- a play on presidential jet Air Force One. With only four weeks until the election, the major investment of time in New Jersey also was designed to give him access to media in neighbouring New York and Pennsylvania.
A state of ticket-splitters, New Jersey usually goes Republican in presidential elections, but it backed Clinton in 1992 and polls show Clinton is well ahead here this year.

Nationally, the latest tracking poll for Reuters by the Zogby Group International released on Tuesday found the race had narrowed considerably to a 5.3 percent margin. Clinton had 43.8 percent to Dole's 38.5 percent among 900 likely voters. Ross Perot had 4.5 percent and 11.3 percent were undecided.
But other recent polls showed Dole with a bigger gap.

In his campaign rallies Dole avoided direct mention of the Whitewater affair and Clinton character issues but in a radio interview with "shock jock" Don Imus on Tuesday morning he referred to the scandal over White House aides getting confidential FBI files.
The bus trip had started out on a fairly upbeat and energetic note Monday, the day after the presidential debate. But the mood seemed to sour along with the weather.
Dole tried to turn it into a joke, standing in the pouring rain and telling supporters that he would add a new tax credit to his list of proposals -- "a rain tax credit."
